cues.text: Let us turn now to the second chapter of this study session: the seven layers of digital transformation.
A common mistake in organisations is to treat digital transformation as a single thing, usually a technology purchase.
In reality, it is a stack of connected responsibilities.
If one is ignored, the others suffer.
This chapter gives you a way of seeing those responsibilities as seven layers.
Look at the table that accompanies this section.
It has three columns.
The first is called Layer.
The second is called Responsibility.
The third is called Failure when neglected.
So for each layer, the table tells you what that layer is responsible for, and what goes wrong if it is ignored.
Let us walk through it row by row, in order.
The first row is the Strategic layer.
Its responsibility is vision, objectives, leadership and investment.
In other words, it answers the questions: where are we going, who is leading us there, and what are we willing to fund?
When this layer is neglected, the failure is technology projects without shared purpose.
Imagine several departments each buying their own software, with no common goal tying those purchases together.
That is what neglected strategy looks like.
The second row is the Business process layer.
Its responsibility is to redesign workflows and eliminate waste.
A workflow is simply the sequence of steps by which work gets done.
When this layer is neglected, the failure is that old bottlenecks remain in digital form.
Think of a paper approval process that needs five signatures.
If you merely scan the form and email it, you still have five waiting points.
You have digitised the bottleneck, not removed it.
The third row is the Technology layer.
Its responsibility covers applications, AI, automation and security.
AI means artificial intelligence, and automation means using systems to carry out tasks with little or no manual effort.
When this layer is neglected, the failure is poor tool fit or unreliable systems.
That means the tools do not match the real need, or they break down when people depend on them.
The fourth row is the Data and integration layer.
Its responsibility is data quality, interoperability and analytics.
Data quality means the data is accurate and usable.
Interoperability means different systems can exchange and understand each other's data.
Analytics means examining data to find useful patterns.
When this layer is neglected, the failure is silos and inconsistent decisions.
A silo is a store of information isolated from the rest of the organisation, so different teams end up working from different versions of the facts.
The fifth row is the Infrastructure layer.
Its responsibility is networks, compute, cloud and storage.
Compute means processing power, and cloud means computing resources delivered over the internet.
When this layer is neglected, the failure is downtime and poor scale.
Downtime is when systems are unavailable, and poor scale means the system cannot cope as demand grows.
The sixth row is the People and culture layer.
Its responsibility is skills, collaboration, adoption and learning.
Adoption means people actually using the new tools and ways of working.
When this layer is neglected, the failure is that staff avoid new workflows.
A perfectly built system that nobody uses delivers nothing.
The seventh and final row is the Customer, or end user, layer.
Its responsibility is accessible, useful experiences and outcomes.
When this layer is neglected, the failure is that customers abandon new services.
If a service is hard to use or does not help people, they simply go back to the old way, or to a competitor.
Now let us see how these layers work together through the example in the source.
A bank wants to offer affordable lending.
Watch how each layer contributes.
Leadership defines the inclusion goal.
That is the strategic layer.
Process owners simplify the applications.
That is the business process layer.
Technology enables digital identity checks.
That is the technology layer.
Data integration brings together relevant records.
That is the data and integration layer.
Resilient infrastructure supports peak demand.
That is the infrastructure layer.
Staff learn new workflows.
That is the people and culture layer.
And customers receive transparent decisions and accessible support.
That is the customer layer.
The source then draws the key lesson: every layer has a dependency on the others.
Remove any one, and the whole effort is weakened.
Brilliant technology cannot rescue a lending product that has no clear goal, and a clear goal cannot succeed on unreliable infrastructure.
Next, let us look more closely at the role of IT, or information technology, in all of this.
The source says IT enables digital business models through connectivity, automation, information, infrastructure and reusable software.
Reusable software means software built once and used again in many places, which saves time and effort.
The source then gives five specific enablers.
First, cloud allows elastic resource allocation.
Elastic means resources can expand or shrink as demand changes, so you use and pay for what you need.
Second, APIs permit controlled integration.
An API, or application programming interface, is an agreed way for one piece of software to request services or data from another, and the control part means access can be limited and governed.
Third, analytics turns records into insights, so stored data becomes a basis for decisions.
Fourth, mobile channels increase reach, meaning you can serve more people in more places.
Fifth, secure payments enable transactions, because people will only buy online if they trust the payment process.
The source concludes that IT can become a strategic capability, not merely administrative support.
Here the distinction matters.
Administrative support means IT simply keeps the office running.
A strategic capability means IT helps create new ways of earning revenue and serving customers.
Finally, let us turn to the digital business model.

According to the source, a digital business model specifies eight things: the value proposition, which is the benefit offered to customers; the customer groups; the channels, meaning how you reach them; the activities; the resources; the partners; the revenues; and the costs.
The source lists common approaches: e-commerce, subscription, freemium, marketplaces and on-demand services.
E-commerce is selling goods or services online.
Subscription means customers pay regularly for continued access.
Freemium offers a basic service free, with paid features for those who want more.
Marketplaces connect buyers and sellers.
On-demand services deliver what the customer wants when they ask for it.
The source also draws a distinction between two structures.
A platform facilitates interactions among participants.
Think of it as a meeting place where different groups find one another.
A pipeline business, by contrast, creates value through a more linear production and distribution chain.
Goods or services move step by step from producer to customer, like water through a pipe.
The source ends with an important qualification: digital businesses can combine models.
A single company might, for example, run a marketplace, offer a subscription tier and provide an on-demand service all together.
So these categories are not rigid boxes.
They are building blocks that organisations may mix.

To bring it together: seven layers, strategic, business process, technology, data and integration, infrastructure, people and culture, and customer, each with its own responsibility and its own characteristic failure.
They depend on one another, IT can serve as a strategic capability across them, and the business model is where all of this turns into a way of creating value.
